name: Canada
summary: A federation formed in 1867 from British North American colonies, now the second-largest country in the world by area. It became fully independent step by step, ending with the Constitution Act of 1982.

knownFor.label: Canadian Pacific Railway
knownFor.note: A railway across the continent that tied British Columbia to the rest of Canada.

knownFor.label: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
knownFor.note: Part of the 1982 constitution; protects basic rights.

knownFor.label: Insulin
knownFor.note: First isolated for medical use at the University of Toronto (Banting and Best).

location.value: Northern North America, from the Atlantic to the Pacific and north into the Arctic; about 10 million km².

terrain.value: The Canadian Shield of ancient rock and lakes, the Prairies, the Rocky Mountains, the Great Lakes–St Lawrence lowlands and Arctic islands.

climate.value: Cold winters almost everywhere; mild on the Pacific coast; Arctic tundra in the north.

resources.value: Timber, furs (historically), wheat, fish, nickel, uranium, potash, oil sands in Alberta and hydroelectric power.

disasters.value: Forest fires, floods, blizzards; the Halifax Explosion (1917) destroyed part of the city.

population.value: About 3.5 million at Confederation (1867); about 41 million today.

urbanisation.value: Most people live within about 200 km of the US border; Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver are the largest cities.

disease.value: Epidemics brought by settlers devastated First Nations earlier; the 1918 influenza; today universal public health care (from the 1960s).

migration.value: Large immigration: British and French at first, then Europeans, and since the 1970s mainly Asians. About a quarter of people were born abroad.

economicBase.value: Farming, timber and mining at first; today services, energy, manufacturing and natural resources.

tradeRoutes.value: Railways across the continent; the St Lawrence Seaway (1959); free trade with the US (1988) and Mexico (1994, NAFTA, now USMCA).

wealth.value: One of the richest countries in the world per person.

moneyAndTax.value: The Canadian dollar; federal and provincial income taxes.

inequality.value: First Nations, Inuit and Métis communities have had lower incomes and worse services; the residential schools (to 1996) caused lasting harm.

governmentType.value: A federal parliamentary democracy and constitutional monarchy, with the British monarch as head of state.

keyRulers.value: John A. Macdonald (first prime minister, 1867). Wilfrid Laurier. Mackenzie King. Pierre Trudeau. Brian Mulroney. Justin Trudeau. Mark Carney (2025).

succession.value: Elections to the House of Commons; the leader of the largest party becomes prime minister.

institutions.value: Parliament in Ottawa, ten provinces and three territories, the Supreme Court, and the Charter of Rights (1982).

stability.value: Stable; Quebec referendums on independence (1980 and 1995) were narrowly rejected. The North-West Rebellion (1885) was put down.

eliteConflict.value: Tension between English- and French-speaking Canada, and between the federal government and provinces (especially Quebec and Alberta).

armyAndTech.value: Small armed forces; large contributions in the World Wars (for example Vimy Ridge in 1917 and Juno Beach in 1944).

majorWars.value: First World War, Second World War, Korean War, the war in Afghanistan; many UN peacekeeping missions.

territoryChange.value: Grew from four provinces to ten (Newfoundland joined in 1949); bought Rupert’s Land from the Hudson’s Bay Company (1870); Nunavut created in 1999.

alliancesRivals.value: Close to Britain and the US; founding member of NATO (1949); member of the Commonwealth and G7.

inventions.value: Insulin (1921), the snowmobile, the Canadarm robotic arm for the Space Shuttle (1981).

scienceEducation.value: Free public schools; universities such as McGill and Toronto; strong research in medicine and AI.

openness.value: Very open to trade and immigration; official multiculturalism since 1971.

religion.value: Mostly Christian (Catholic and Protestant) historically; growing numbers with no religion, and Muslim, Hindu and Sikh communities.

languageWriting.value: English and French are the two official languages (1969); also many Indigenous languages, such as Cree and Inuktitut.

artsArchitecture.value: The Group of Seven painters, Indigenous art, a strong film and music industry.

socialStructure.value: A large middle class; historic inequality for Indigenous peoples.

sharedIdentity.value: A bilingual, multicultural identity, often defined partly in contrast with the United States.

neighbours.value: The United States (the world’s longest land border shared by two countries) and Greenland (Denmark) across the sea.

ideasReligions.value: British parliamentary traditions; French civil law in Quebec; Christian missions; later ideas of multiculturalism.

colonisation.value: Itself a former British dominion; it settled the West on lands of First Nations through treaties that are still debated.

riseSignals.value: Confederation in 1867 united the colonies to defend against US expansion and to build railways.

peakPeriod.value: After 1945: rapid growth, a welfare state, and full control over its constitution (1982).

declineSignals.value: Debates over national unity (Quebec) and the treatment of Indigenous peoples.

sources.value: Wikipedia: Canada; Wikipedia: History of Canada; Statistics Canada census figures.
